reviews.title: The Invite
reviews.deck: Olivia Wilde’s full-length directorial debut *Booksmart* (2019) announced her as a strong talent behind the camera.
reviews.author: Chad Durham
reviews.body:
Olivia Wilde’s full-length directorial debut *Booksmart* (2019) announced her as a strong talent behind the camera. Critics and audiences responded well to the funny and reflective movie about teen best friends on the eve of their high school graduation. However, Wilde’s next directorial effort, *Don’t Worry Darling* (2022), though ambitious and starring a great cast, was widely panned and, for some, considered a step back. So it is heartening to see the success and dexterity of her latest. *The Invite* is a humorous, mature, seriously entertaining drama that finds thoughtful things to say about marriage, communication, and keys to understanding others.

The story concerns married couple Joe (Seth Rogen) and Angela (Olivia Wilde), who have a little strain showing in their marriage. Since their daughter is away at a sleepover, Angela has invited the couple who lives above them, Piña (Penelope Cruz) and Hawk (Edward Norton), over for dinner. Once the couples get together, the discussions between these distinct personalities take the night in surprising directions.

The script, from Rashida Jones and Will McCormack (and based on Cesc Gay’s screenplay for *The People Upstairs*) is shrewd. The movie feels like a play, mostly staying in one location–Angela and Joe’s apartment–and hinging almost entirely on dialogue. Though this can often halt a movie’s dynamism, here it narrows the focus with insight. It avoids obvious punchlines, sidesteps clichés, and slyly reveals interesting things about each character and their motivations. Wilde’s direction, as well, is assured, utilizing the cinematography by Adam Newport-Berra to seamlessly enhance the humor and melancholy. They symbolically shoot through windows often, giving the sense that the audience is spying on private things and they deftly employ crucial close-ups to excavate emotion. The camera work never overshadows the story, but serves it productively. And Wilde coaxes disciplined but diverse performances from her talented cast.

Those performances are stellar across the board. Without the principals injecting realism and clarity, the movie would feel much more stagey. Rogen, known as an effective comedic presence, is subtler here and weaponizes his schlubby persona to singular effect. Part of the strength of Joe comes from the audience’s expectations of what Rogen normally portrays. The depth he plumbs here may catch some viewers off-guard. Likewise, Cruz’s role deepens as the movie progresses and she showcases her veteran presence with surprising ease, managing to deliver some of the movie’s biggest themes without a drop of artifice. Norton balances his tone of voice and facial expressions to suggest Hawk’s intriguing vision and confusion. Those are not easy contrasts to adequately convey simultaneously. Finally, Wilde does not let sitting in the director’s chair overshadow her performance in the movie. Angela’s angst and dissatisfaction must feel authentic for the audience to care about her relationship. Wilde’s subtle body language and reasonable reactions connect the audience to her key feelings.

The biggest strength of *The Invite*, ultimately, is its confidence. As every member of the cast imbues their role with realism and depth, every piece of dialogue and turn of the story is calculated for what it reveals about the two couples, and every shot–no matter how simple or showy–seems to have a purpose. It is true that some movies have noticeable conviction unsupported by the flimsiness of what they present. Here, Wilde and her team reveal interesting and rich truths through the accurate belief that they have made something valuable. *The Invite* will last as a comedic and dramatic triumph, likely leading to multiple Oscar nominations.

reviews.title: The Odyssey
reviews.deck: The Odyssey is an impressive piece of filmmaking, anchored by exceptional performances and a dynamite script and elevated by all of the craftspeople who helped bring it to life.
reviews.author: Chad Durham
reviews.body:
Christopher Nolan is one of the greatest American directors. He has honed his knack for corralling cerebral, big-budget dramas into enjoyable but controlled productions. The challenge seems to fuel him.  His latest, an adaptation of Homer’s The Odyssey, is no exception. Nolan has once again established a clear vision and translated it masterfully to the screen. The Odyssey is an impressive piece of filmmaking, anchored by exceptional performances and a dynamite script and elevated by all of the craftspeople who helped bring it to life.

Simply put, the story is of Odysseus (Matt Damon), king of Ithaca, who left home to fight the Trojan War and has not returned. In his absence, various suitors who believe he will never return are hoping to marry Odysseus’ wife, Penelope (Anne Hathaway).  She and Odysseus’ son, Telemachus (Tom Holland), who was extremely young when his father left and does not really know him, is grappling with his place on the island and in the world. The plot presents many different characters in Ithaca’s and Odysseus’ tapestry, focusing on relationships and myriad motives.

Those characters are brought to life in a multitude of potent performances, all imbuing the fantastic elements of Homer’s story with realism and relevant emotional depth. It may feature the highest quality of acting of any of Nolan’s movies. Damon commands respect as Odysseus, but also finds shades of emotion to showcase his human side. Hathaway gives one of the greatest performances of her career as Penelope. She resists an easy caricature of a wife that lacks purpose because she is pining for her lost husband. Instead, she uses her expressive eyes and face to project both steely resolve and a dimming hope for the future of her family and her city. 

Samantha Morton’s performance as Circe had generated substantial buzz before the movie even hit theaters and it is easy to see why. Though Morton has been doing incredible work for years, her nuanced portrayal here (in very limited screen time) is fantastic. She makes an indelible mark with casually intense line readings and body language that suggests a lifetime of being weighed down by the cruelty of fate and a  misogynistic society. Morton has the responsibility of making mystical moments feel lived-in and rational and does so with aplomb. Likewise, John Leguizamo’s supporting performance as the blind Eumaeus is beautiful. He conveys all of his worry and pride and wisdom thoughtfully. His thematic importance is highlighted by his warm but prickly persona. Leguizamo is a revelation.

But none of the performances would be as fully realized without a strong script. It accomplishes the tricky task of relaying the mythological story in a human and personal way. Nolan still includes Cyclops and the sirens and humans being transformed into animals but in the context of what it means for the characters and how viewers can apply the lessons in their own lives. He also uses modern dialogue but it manages to feel fluid and organic. One of the movie’s most exquisite traits is not keeping the audience at arm’s length. Its clarity and allure stay maintained throughout.

No surprise, the rest of the moviemaking is close to brilliant. Ludwig Goransson’s score does not use an orchestra as he and Nolan felt that would be true to the world they were representing. Nolan also challenged Goransson to use bronze as a thematic element. This all adds up to a singular sound that enhances the atmosphere of the film. Hoyte van Hoytema’s cinematography–entirely on IMAX cameras–is visceral and hard-hitting, creating a larger-than-life aesthetic on battlefields and an intimacy in the more raw, emotional moments. The movie is an outsized spectacle, yet it finds a way to cohere so fully in its conclusion.

At this point, it is almost too conventional to praise a Nolan film. His last movie, Oppenheimer, won seven Academy Awards including Best Director and Best Picture. Being so great for so long can lead viewers to experience a bit of a letdown when they see his newest picture. That is what makes The Odyssey such a treasure: with sky-high expectations to tell a story that has been around for thousands of years, Nolan and his squad have still made a remarkable movie. The Odyssey resonates with significant ideas about war, ego, leadership, and timeworn romance. It expounds on what it means to be a soldier and what it means to be beholden to a higher power. It will retain relevance and entrance audiences for years to come.

Check out Chad’s [short TikTok](https://www.tiktok.com/@enjoyingthefilm/video/7665527296056446238) about The Odyssey.

reviews.title: Tony
reviews.deck: *Tony* is engrossing, thoughtful, and extremely well acted and manages to teach its audience many things about Bourdain while still leaving the remainder of his life completely untouched
reviews.author: Chad Durham
reviews.body:
Biopics often fall into traps. Sometimes, they want to include so much about the subject of the film that they move too quickly, glossing over much and settling for breadth over quality. Other times, they completely leave out essential parts of the subject’s life because they just don’t have the time to add everything. Still other times, there is a hollowness to the proceedings because the actors and writers simply cannot do justice to the scope or size of the woman they are trying to sum up. This absolutely does not make every biopic ineffective, it just makes creating a forceful one a difficult prospect. This is what makes *Tony*, the film about Anthony Bourdain, directed by Matt Johnson, so captivating. The movie focuses on just the 1975 summer months when the 19-year-old Bourdain travels to Provincetown, Massachusetts to chase after a girl. It manages to say much about being human and growing up in very little time. *Tony* is engrossing, thoughtful, and extremely well acted and manages to teach its audience many things about Bourdain while still leaving the remainder of his life completely untouched.

First off, the script is a revelation, managing to skirt formula even when it takes steps that seem to telegraph where it is going. Though there is a “mentor figure” and a romantic side plot, Johnson and his three other screenplay collaborators do a deft job of handling those seemingly conventional ideas with depth and insight. They also underline the relevance of Bourdain’s experiences without resorting to characters parroting the themes to the audience in stilted dialogue. A huge strength of the script is its lack of arrogance. Though Bourdain is often an appealing and sympathetic figure, he is also humorously misguided, as 19-year-olds often are. The writers are content to allow him to reflect earnest human experience until very late in the film. Treating Bourdain like a perfect rebel or a bulletproof hero would have built up a mythos, but would have rung untrue. Seeing this man in a clear way allows the themes to burrow themselves into the viewers’ hearts.

The acting in *Tony* is also subtle and sharp. Dominic Sessa plays the college-age Bourdain and avoids obvious pitfalls in playing a character who is an arrogant jackass who expects the cards to always fall in his favor. The script provides reasoning for why he is the way he is, but Sessa imbues him with realism and charm and makes it hard not to root for him, even when he makes questionable choices. Antonio Banderas is wonderful as Bourdain’s quasi-mentor José Vatel (usually called “Chef”). He uses his face exquisitely in a quiet performance, which only increases in power as the movie progresses. Emilia Jones is perhaps not given enough to do, but she seizes the opportunities presented to her, leaving a strong impression when she could easily have faded into the background. Leo Woodall, who has previously been wonderful in *The White Lotus*, *One Day*, and *Tuner*, continues to show what an impressive actor he is. Here, he is often a bad influence over Bourdain, but his line delivery and presence make him a charismatic centerpoint every time he is onscreen. These performers elevate the effective script with aplomb.

In short, if you have a chance to see *Tony*, I highly recommend it. It says a lot about figuring life out and not following a preordained path without ever hitting the audience over the head. Its quiet conclusion is much more affecting than many emotional, overwrought Hollywood endings. Everyone makes massive mistakes before they ever find their path and watching Anthony Bourdain commit a lot of errors will resonate with many viewers, both those that have found their life’s stability and those still navigating life’s pitfalls.

reviews.title: Spider-Man: Brand New Day Review
reviews.deck: Spider-Man: Brand New Day is a welcome breath of fresh air
reviews.author: Chad Durham
reviews.body:
Superhero and comic-book fatigue is a real thing. There were 22 Marvel Cinematic Universe (MCU) films before *Avengers: Endgame* hit theaters. *Endgame* made about $2.8 billion internationally and brought the initial phase of the MCU to a satisfying and thoughtful close. Since then, however, Marvel comic-book movies have been less successful monetarily and less celebrated critically. Some of that stems from Marvel (and its hired filmmakers) not being able to cover much new ground thematically or storywise. And some stems from the fact that the audience is just a little tired of more superhero movies. That is why –on a small scale– *Spider-Man: Brand New Day* is a welcome breath of fresh air. It manages to ground its story in real emotion and allow characters’ motives to overrule spectacle for the majority of its running time. Though it still sometimes falls into familiar comic-book traps and tropes, it is an effective time at the movies.

The story picks up where *No Way Home* left off, with Peter (Tom Holland) no longer having a relationship with his friends and being left to fight criminals with no one to support him. This causes loneliness and isolation, as one might expect. Peter also deals with some unexpected physical changes, which allows the movie to explore some interesting themes about mental and physical health.

The performances in the Tom Holland Spider-Man series have always been quite good. That continues in *Brand New Day*. Tom Holland shows more understated levels as Peter Parker deals with watching the lives of his former girlfriend MJ (Zendaya) and his former best friend and “guy in the chair” Ned (Jacob Batalon), who no longer know who he is. He cogently anchors the movie, resisting the urge to “phone it in” in his fourth Spider-Man adventure. Zendaya and Batalon also feast on the new opportunity to show what their characters' real lives would look like without being connected to Spider-Man.

Though *Brand New Day* does feature appearances by some other Marvel superheroes, it still succeeds in not feeling like a product that had studio-mandated cameos and tangents. There is logic in the screenplay for every one of them showing up, and they all affect the story in meaningful ways. Florence Pugh, Mark Ruffalo, and Jon Bernthal are all fantastic in these roles, seizing moments big and small and staying true to their characters.

The bottom line is that *Brand New Day* grounds its superhero shenanigans in well-earned emotion and realistic consequences. There is still humor, which lacks contrivance. There are multiple occasions that elicit surprising dismay, as they feel less like they come from a friendly comic-book construction and more like they come from ill-advised human decisions. And, ultimately, the movie earns goodwill from its viewers by caring about the characters instead of forcing them through a hamster wheel of fanboy-mandated material.
